items.stem: Which of the following best describes "millennium"?
options: A roadside inn with a courtyard where merchants and their animals rested on Silk Road routes
Printing by carving a whole page in reverse on a wooden block, inking it and pressing paper onto it
A complex society with cities, organised government, specialised jobs, social classes, writing and monumental buildings
items.answer: A period of 1 000 years
items.markingKey: D. "millennium" is a period of 1 000 years.

items.stem: Nia writes: "If one event comes before another, the first must have caused the second." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sequence is not cause: historians need evidence of a link before claiming causation.
items.markingKey: Sequence is not cause: historians need evidence of a link before claiming causation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between causation and chronology.
items.answer: Chronology is the order in which events happened; causation is why they happened and how one event led to another – an earlier event is not automatically a cause.
items.markingKey: Chronology is the order in which events happened; causation is why they happened and how one event led to another – an earlier event is not automatically a cause. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why dates BCE get smaller as time moves forward.
items.answer: BCE years are counted backwards from the start of the Common Era, so an event in 300 BCE is earlier than one in 200 BCE, and the numbers decrease towards 1 BCE.
items.markingKey: Content: BCE years are counted backwards from the start of the Common Era, so an event in 300 BCE is earlier than one in 200 BCE, and the numbers decrease towards 1 BCE. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Explain why "How did the Egyptian calendar of three seasons reflect the annual flooding of the Nile?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into chronology, BCE/CE dating and timelines.
items.answer: It links chronology and time-keeping to geography and has accessible primary and secondary evidence.
items.markingKey: It links chronology and time-keeping to geography and has accessible primary and secondary evidence. items.stem:
Source A – Ancient history (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Herodotus, "The Histories", Book II, written c. 430 BCE

The Greek writer described Egypt as a land made by the river: each year the Nile flooded the fields, and when the waters went down the Egyptians sowed their crops in the rich mud it left behind.

With reference to its origin and purpose, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a student investigating chronology, BCE/CE dating and timelines.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Herodotus, "The Histories", Book II, written c. 430 BCE. Purpose: to describe Egypt and its customs for a Greek audience. Value: An early outsider's description, written more than 2 000 years after the pyramids were built, that shows how ancient writers understood the Nile. Limitation: Herodotus visited Egypt centuries after the Old Kingdom and relied partly on what priests told him, so his chronology is not reliable.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of Herodotus, "The Histories", Book II, written c. 430 BCE. Purpose: to describe Egypt and its customs for a Greek audience. Value: An early outsider's description, written more than 2 000 years after the pyramids were built, that shows how ancient writers understood the Nile. Limitation: Herodotus visited Egypt centuries after the Old Kingdom and relied partly on what priests told him, so his chronology is not reliable. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". items.stem: In which century is the year 1066?
items.answer: The 11th century CE
items.markingKey: C. 1001–1100 is the 11th century.

items.stem: Explain why a timeline needs a consistent scale.
items.answer: If equal distances do not represent equal amounts of time, the timeline gives a misleading impression of how close or far apart events were.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If equal distances do not represent equal amounts of time, the timeline gives a misleading impression of how close or far apart events were. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Priya argues that "Learning dates is the most important skill in history." Yusuf disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Disagree: secure chronology is a foundation, but the key historical skills are explaining, interpreting and evaluating – dates serve those skills.
items.markingKey: Priya: chronology lets historians see sequence, change and continuity. Yusuf: interpreting evidence and explaining causes matter more than memorising dates. Judgement (1-2 marks): Disagree: secure chronology is a foundation, but the key historical skills are explaining, interpreting and evaluating – dates serve those skills.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Learning dates is the most important skill in history."
items.answer: Thesis: Disagree: secure chronology is a foundation, but the key historical skills are explaining, interpreting and evaluating – dates serve those skills.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: chronology lets historians see sequence, change and continuity; without dates causation cannot be judged. Counter-arguments: interpreting evidence and explaining causes matter more than memorising dates; many dates are approximate. Thesis/conclusion: Disagree: secure chronology is a foundation, but the key historical skills are explaining, interpreting and evaluating – dates serve those skills. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "surplus"?
options: "Before the Common Era": years counted backwards before the traditional birth year of Jesus, equivalent to BC
"Common Era": years counted forwards from year 1, equivalent to AD
More food than a farming community needs to survive, allowing some people to do other jobs
A period of 100 years; the 15th century CE runs from 1401 to 1500
items.answer: More food than a farming community needs to survive, allowing some people to do other jobs
items.markingKey: C. "surplus" is more food than a farming community needs to survive, allowing some people to do other jobs.

items.stem: Explain why historians still know less about the Indus civilisation than about Egypt.
items.answer: The Indus script has not been deciphered, so we cannot read their own records; knowledge comes mostly from archaeology.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Indus script has not been deciphered, so we cannot read their own records; knowledge comes mostly from archaeology. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an empire and a city-state.
items.answer: A city-state is one city and its surrounding land with its own ruler (e.g. Ur); an empire is a large area including many peoples ruled by one power (e.g. Akkad under Sargon).
items.markingKey: A city-state is one city and its surrounding land with its own ruler (e.g. Ur); an empire is a large area including many peoples ruled by one power (e.g. Akkad under Sargon). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "Ancient Egypt depended on regular rain for farming." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Egypt receives very little rain; farming depended on the annual Nile flood and irrigation.
items.markingKey: Egypt receives very little rain; farming depended on the annual Nile flood and irrigation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why "What does the town planning of Mohenjo-daro suggest about how the Indus civilisation was organised?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into river valley civilisations of the Indus, Mesopotamia, Egypt and China.
items.answer: It uses archaeological evidence to investigate an open historical question about an undeciphered civilisation.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "civilisation".
items.answer: A complex society with cities, organised government, specialised jobs, social classes, writing and monumental buildings
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a complex society with cities, organised government, specialised jobs, social classes, writing and monumental buildings. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "The pyramids were built by enslaved prisoners of war." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Evidence from workers' villages at Giza suggests organised, paid and fed labour crews, including seasonal farmers; slavery existed in Egypt but did not build the pyramids in the way often shown in films.
items.markingKey: Evidence from workers' villages at Giza suggests organised, paid and fed labour crews, including seasonal farmers; slavery existed in Egypt but did not build the pyramids in the way often shown in films. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – Law code (paraphrased): Paraphrase of laws 196, 198 and 199 of the Code of Hammurabi, Babylon, c. 1754 BCE (stele now in the Louvre, Paris)

If a free man destroys the eye of another free man, his own eye shall be destroyed. If he destroys the eye of a commoner, he shall pay one mina of silver. If he destroys the eye of a man's slave, he shall pay half the slave's value.

Identify two points that Source A makes about river valley civilisations of the Indus, Mesopotamia, Egypt and China, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: Punishments in Babylon depended on the social class of the victim.
items.markingKey: Punishments in Babylon depended on the social class of the victim. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Rivers were the single most important reason why the first civilisations developed." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Rivers were a necessary condition, but not sufficient: civilisation also needed social organisation, technology and trade.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: all four early civilisations grew in river valleys; rivers gave water, silt and transport needed for a food surplus. Counter-arguments: organisation, leadership and religion turned farming villages into cities; trade and technology such as writing and bronze were also essential. Thesis/conclusion: Rivers were a necessary condition, but not sufficient: civilisation also needed social organisation, technology and trade. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. items.stem: Which religion spread from India along the Silk Road to China?
items.answer: Buddhism
items.markingKey: Buddhism. Buddhist monasteries and cave temples such as Mogao at Dunhuang lie on the routes.

items.stem: Distinguish between the maritime Silk Road and the overland Silk Road.
items.answer: The overland routes crossed deserts and mountains by camel caravan; the maritime routes used monsoon winds to sail between China, South-east Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa and could carry bulkier goods.
items.markingKey: The overland routes crossed deserts and mountains by camel caravan; the maritime routes used monsoon winds to sail between China, South-east Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa and could carry bulkier goods. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the Silk Road was as important for ideas as for goods.
items.answer: Travellers carried religions, languages, art styles, scientific knowledge and technologies such as papermaking, which changed societies along the way.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Travellers carried religions, languages, art styles, scientific knowledge and technologies such as papermaking, which changed societies along the way. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "The exchange of ideas along the Silk Road was more important than the exchange of goods." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Ideas had the longest-lasting impact, but they travelled because of the trade in goods – the two cannot really be separated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: religions such as Buddhism and Islam spread and lasted for centuries; technologies like paper changed learning and government. Thesis/conclusion: Ideas had the longest-lasting impact, but they travelled because of the trade in goods – the two cannot really be separated. items.stem:
Source A – Travel account (paraphrased): Paraphrase of "The Travels of Marco Polo", written down by Rustichello da Pisa c. 1298

The traveller described the Great Khan's paper money, made from the bark of mulberry trees and stamped with the ruler's seal. Everyone in the empire had to accept it in payment, and merchants exchanged their gold, pearls and precious stones for it.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the Silk Road: its trade routes, goods, ideas and religions. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of "The Travels of Marco Polo", written down by Rustichello da Pisa c. 1298. Purpose: to describe the wonders of the East for European readers and entertain them. Value: It is one of the few European eyewitness accounts of Mongol China and describes a real Yuan institution, paper money. Limitation: It was written years later with a co-author who wrote romances, so some details may be exaggerated; some historians question parts of it.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of "The Travels of Marco Polo", written down by Rustichello da Pisa c. 1298. Purpose: to describe the wonders of the East for European readers and entertain them. items.stem: In which city was an early paper mill established in about 794 CE, spreading paper across the Islamic world?
items.answer: Baghdad

items.stem: Distinguish between invention and diffusion.
items.answer: Invention is the creation of a new technology in one place; diffusion is its spread from that place to other societies.
items.markingKey: Invention is the creation of a new technology in one place; diffusion is its spread from that place to other societies. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: 689 years

items.answer: The period of relative peace across the Mongol Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries that made long-distance trade safer

items.stem: A student claims: "The year 1500 is in the 16th century." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.stem: Explain why controlling floods and irrigation could increase the power of rulers.

items.stem: Explain why the Hindu–Arabic numeral system replaced Roman numerals for calculation in Europe.
items.answer: Place value and zero made addition, multiplication and accounting far easier; merchants and bankers adopted it, although some cities at first banned it in official records for fear of fraud.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Place value and zero made addition, multiplication and accounting far easier; merchants and bankers adopted it, although some cities at first banned it in official records for fear of fraud. items.stem: Arjun writes: "Only silk was traded along the Silk Road." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Spices, horses, glass, gold, silver, jade, porcelain, paper and many other goods were traded, along with ideas.
items.markingKey: Spices, horses, glass, gold, silver, jade, porcelain, paper and many other goods were traded, along with ideas. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to radiocarbon dating of the Indus city of Mohenjo-daro, explain how it illustrates how historians date the distant past.
items.answer: Dates from organic remains place its mature phase at about 2500–1900 BCE. Scientific methods give approximate dates, so ancient chronology is written with "c.".
items.markingKey: Context (Dates from organic remains place its mature phase at about 2500–1900 BCE.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: scientific methods give approximate dates, so ancient chronology is written with "c.". – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how historians date the distant past.

items.stem: Zara argues that "Rivers were the single most important reason why the first civilisations developed." Elena disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Rivers were a necessary condition, but not sufficient: civilisation also needed social organisation, technology and trade.
items.markingKey: Zara: all four early civilisations grew in river valleys. Elena: organisation, leadership and religion turned farming villages into cities. Judgement (1-2 marks): Rivers were a necessary condition, but not sufficient: civilisation also needed social organisation, technology and trade.

items.stem: Lukas argues that "Paper was the most important technology to travel along the Silk Road." Tomás disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: A strong case, because paper underpinned learning, government and printing, but gunpowder and numerals had equally deep effects in other areas.
items.markingKey: Lukas: it made books and records cheaper and spread learning and bureaucracy. Tomás: gunpowder transformed warfare and the power of states. Judgement (1-2 marks): A strong case, because paper underpinned learning, government and printing, but gunpowder and numerals had equally deep effects in other areas.

items.stem: Maya argues that "The exchange of ideas along the Silk Road was more important than the exchange of goods." Elena disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Ideas had the longest-lasting impact, but they travelled because of the trade in goods – the two cannot really be separated.
items.markingKey: Maya: religions such as Buddhism and Islam spread and lasted for centuries. Elena: trade in goods made cities rich and paid for the journeys that carried ideas. Judgement (1-2 marks): Ideas had the longest-lasting impact, but they travelled because of the trade in goods – the two cannot really be separated.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How did the Egyptian calendar of three seasons reflect the annual flooding of the Nile?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Read museum websites (British Museum, Met) and a textbook; record the three seasons (Akhet, Peret, Shemu) and their months; compare with Nile flood data; create a timeline; cite sources in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Read museum websites (British Museum, Met) and a textbook; record the three seasons (Akhet, Peret, Shemu) and their months; compare with Nile flood data; create a timeline; cite sources in MLA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What was life like in the past?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into river valley civilisations of the Indus, Mesopotamia, Egypt and China. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is far too broad: no civilisation, time or aspect is named Improved: "What does the town planning of Mohenjo-daro suggest about how the Indus civilisation was organised?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is far too broad: no civilisation, time or aspect is named); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "What does the town planning of Mohenjo-daro suggest about how the Indus civilisation was organised?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the Hindu–Arabic numeral system replaced Roman numerals for calculation in Europe.
items.answer: Place value and zero made addition, multiplication and accounting far easier; merchants and bankers adopted it, although some cities at first banned it in official records for fear of fraud.
items.markingKey: Content: Place value and zero made addition, multiplication and accounting far easier; merchants and bankers adopted it, although some cities at first banned it in official records for fear of fraud. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The exchange of ideas along the Silk Road was more important than the exchange of goods."
items.answer: Ideas had the longest-lasting impact, but they travelled because of the trade in goods – the two cannot really be separated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: religions such as Buddhism and Islam spread and lasted for centuries; technologies like paper changed learning and government. Arguments against: trade in goods made cities rich and paid for the journeys that carried ideas; disease also spread, causing the Black Death. Supported judgement: Ideas had the longest-lasting impact, but they travelled because of the trade in goods – the two cannot really be separated.

items.stem:
Source A – Ancient history (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Herodotus, "The Histories", Book II, written c. 430 BCE

The Greek writer described Egypt as a land made by the river: each year the Nile flooded the fields, and when the waters went down the Egyptians sowed their crops in the rich mud it left behind.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Learning dates is the most important skill in history."
items.answer: Disagree: secure chronology is a foundation, but the key historical skills are explaining, interpreting and evaluating – dates serve those skills.
items.markingKey: From the source: Egyptian farming and civilisation depended on the annual Nile flood. Own knowledge for: chronology lets historians see sequence, change and continuity; without dates causation cannot be judged. Own knowledge against: interpreting evidence and explaining causes matter more than memorising dates; many dates are approximate. Judgement: Disagree: secure chronology is a foundation, but the key historical skills are explaining, interpreting and evaluating – dates serve those skills. items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How did the arrival of paper change the way books were produced in Baghdad between 750 and 900 CE?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Read two scholarly articles and a museum resource on Abbasid manuscripts; take Cornell notes; build a timeline; compare costs of papyrus, parchment and paper; cite sources; evaluate gaps in evidence.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Read two scholarly articles and a museum resource on Abbasid manuscripts; take Cornell notes; build a timeline; compare costs of papyrus, parchment and paper; cite sources; evaluate gaps in evidence. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A roadside inn with a courtyard where merchants and their animals rested on Silk Road routes"?
items.answer: caravanserai
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of caravanserai.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A Latin word meaning "about", used before an approximate date"?
items.answer: circa (c.)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of circa (c.).

items.stem: Which river valley was home to China's Shang dynasty?
items.answer: The Huang He (Yellow River)
items.markingKey: The Huang He (Yellow River). The Shang ruled c. 1600–1046 BCE.

items.stem: Distinguish between woodblock printing and movable-type printing.
items.answer: Woodblock printing carves a whole page into one block; movable type uses separate reusable characters that can be rearranged – first in China (Bi Sheng, 1040s), Korea (metal type) and later Europe (Gutenberg, c. 1450).
items.markingKey: Woodblock printing carves a whole page into one block; movable type uses separate reusable characters that can be rearranged – first in China (Bi Sheng, 1040s), Korea (metal type) and later Europe (Gutenberg, c. 1450). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Spices, horses, glass, gold, silver, jade, porcelain, paper and many other goods were traded, along with ideas.
items.markingKey: Spices, horses, glass, gold, silver, jade, porcelain, paper and many other goods were traded, along with ideas. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between causation and chronology.
items.answer: Chronology is the order in which events happened; causation is why they happened and how one event led to another – an earlier event is not automatically a cause.
items.markingKey: Chronology is the order in which events happened; causation is why they happened and how one event led to another – an earlier event is not automatically a cause. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the Indus Valley civilisation and the Egyptian civilisation.
items.answer: Egypt had powerful god-kings (pharaohs), monumental tombs and readable hieroglyphs; the Indus cities show careful planning and drains but no grand palaces or royal tombs, and their script is undeciphered.
items.markingKey: Egypt had powerful god-kings (pharaohs), monumental tombs and readable hieroglyphs; the Indus cities show careful planning and drains but no grand palaces or royal tombs, and their script is undeciphered. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Gunpowder was first invented in Europe for cannons." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It was developed in China, where a formula appears in a military text of 1044, and spread west by the 13th century.
items.markingKey: It was developed in China, where a formula appears in a military text of 1044, and spread west by the 13th century. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars writes: "The Silk Road only helped Europe." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Central Asian cities, Persia, India and China all grew rich from the trade and exchanged ideas in all directions.
items.markingKey: Central Asian cities, Persia, India and China all grew rich from the trade and exchanged ideas in all directions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Place these events in chronological order, earliest first: Marco Polo reaches the court of Kublai Khan (approx.) (1275 CE); the reign of Hammurabi of Babylon begins (approx.) (1792 BCE); the death of Julius Caesar (44 BCE); the reign of Ashoka begins (approx.) (268 BCE).
items.answer: the reign of Hammurabi of Babylon begins (approx.) → the reign of Ashoka begins (approx.) → the death of Julius Caesar → Marco Polo reaches the court of Kublai Khan (approx.)

items.stem:
Source A – Law code (paraphrased): Paraphrase of laws 196, 198 and 199 of the Code of Hammurabi, Babylon, c. 1754 BCE (stele now in the Louvre, Paris)

If a free man destroys the eye of another free man, his own eye shall be destroyed. If he destroys the eye of a commoner, he shall pay one mina of silver. If he destroys the eye of a man's slave, he shall pay half the slave's value.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about river valley civilisations of the Indus, Mesopotamia, Egypt and China. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of laws 196, 198 and 199 of the Code of Hammurabi, Babylon, c. 1754 BCE (stele now in the Louvre, Paris). Purpose: to set out the king's laws and show Hammurabi as a just ruler chosen by the gods. Value: It is an original primary source from the ruler himself and reveals the social classes of Babylon. Limitation: It shows the laws as written, not how they were applied in real courts; it presents an idealised royal image.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of laws 196, 198 and 199 of the Code of Hammurabi, Babylon, c. 1754 BCE (stele now in the Louvre, Paris). Limitation: It shows the laws as written, not how they were applied in real courts; it presents an idealised royal image. items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into cultural exchange and the spread of technologies such as paper, gunpowder and numerals?
options: What was traded on the Silk Road?
How did the arrival of paper change the way books were produced in Baghdad between 750 and 900 CE?
What was life like in the past?
items.answer: How did the arrival of paper change the way books were produced in Baghdad between 750 and 900 CE?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: With reference to the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang, explain how it illustrates cultural exchange on the Silk Road.
items.answer: Hundreds of Buddhist cave temples were cut and painted between the 4th and 14th centuries at this oasis town; a hidden library held thousands of manuscripts in many languages. Indian, Central Asian and Chinese art styles and texts met at one oasis on the route.
items.markingKey: Context (Hundreds of Buddhist cave temples were cut and painted between the 4th and 14th centuries at this oasis town; a hidden library held thousands of manuscripts in many languages.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Indian, Central Asian and Chinese art styles and texts met at one oasis on the route. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cultural exchange on the Silk Road.

items.stem: How many years passed between the death of Julius Caesar (44 BCE) and the Battle of Panipat that founded Mughal rule (1526 CE)?
items.answer: 1569 years
items.markingKey: 44 + 1526 − 1 = 1569 (subtract 1 because there is no year 0) (M1 A1). BCE years count down towards 1 BCE; the year after 1 BCE is 1 CE.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Code of Hammurabi and explain what it reveals about law and social hierarchy in Mesopotamia.
items.answer: Nearly 300 laws carved on a basalt stele set out punishments that varied by social class. It shows a ruler using written law to keep order and claim justice, and that society was divided into classes.
items.markingKey: Context (Nearly 300 laws carved on a basalt stele set out punishments that varied by social class.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows a ruler using written law to keep order and claim justice, and that society was divided into classes. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to law and social hierarchy in Mesopotamia.
